brief.greeting: Good morning. The Linux kernel slipped another prepatch while a keyboard rode a conveyor belt.

stories.headline: 7.3‑rc6 prepatch lands, no schedule shift
stories.body: **Prepatch released for testing:** Linux 7.3‑rc6 is out for developers, and it doesn’t push back the expected release timeline.
stories.why: You can test new kernel bits without fearing a missed deadline.

stories.headline: Google Japan ships conveyor‑belt keyboard prototype
stories.body: **Keys on a moving belt:** The GBoard prototype uses a tiny conveyor to feed keys to your fingers, with firmware and STL files posted on GitHub.
stories.why: It shows how mechanical tricks can simplify ergonomic design.

stories.headline: 8‑bit AVR laptop runs video, audio, multitask
stories.body: **8‑bit notebook proves its mettle:** An AVR‑based laptop streams video, plays audio, and multitasks, rivaling far newer boards.
stories.why: It reminds you that raw clock speed isn’t everything for embedded projects.

quick_hits.text: **Inference engines:** DeepSeek 4 Flash now supports Metal, CUDA, ROCm.
**Web server:** Caddy auto‑HTTPS makes TLS painless.
**Error tracking:** Sentry offers open‑source performance monitoring.
**Belt game:** BlobJump uses a moving belt to get you moving.

brief.sign_off: That’s your tech bite. See you tomorrow

highlights.title: Kernel prepatch 7.3-rc6
highlights.summary: The Linux 7.3‑rc6 kernel prepatch has been published for testing, with no expected impact on the overall release schedule.
highlights.detail: Linus Torvalds noted upcoming maintainer summit and Linux Plumbers Conference may affect merge statistics, but the timeline remains stable. Developers are encouraged to test the prepatch and report regressions before the next rc.

highlights.title: Conveyor Belt GBoard Brings the Keys to You
highlights.summary: Google Japan unveiled a conveyor‑belt keyboard prototype, with firmware and STL files released on GitHub.
highlights.detail: The design continuously moves keys toward the user, creating a novel typing experience that challenges conventional ergonomics. All design files are open source, allowing hobbyists to build or modify the system.

highlights.title: tester-army/e2e
highlights.summary: tester-army/e2e is a next‑generation end‑to‑end testing framework for web and mobile applications.
highlights.detail: The framework targets modern development workflows, offering cross‑platform support and integration with popular CI pipelines, but specific performance metrics are not disclosed.

highlights.title: antirez/ds4
highlights.summary: antirez/ds4 provides DeepSeek 4 Flash and PRO inference engines for Metal, CUDA, and ROCm.
highlights.detail: These engines enable local AI model inference on various hardware accelerators, supporting both Apple and GPU ecosystems without requiring cloud resources.

highlights.title: azahar-emu/azahar
highlights.summary: azahar-emu/azahar is an open‑source Nintendo 3DS emulator built on the Citra codebase.
highlights.detail: Implemented in C++, the project aims to provide a lightweight alternative to Citra, focusing on compatibility and performance for 3DS titles.

items.title: Model: ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF
items.summary: The ISTA-DASLab Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO model for image-to-text is available in GGUF format and has been downloaded 1,886,975 times.
items.detail: The model targets image‑text‑to‑text tasks and is hosted on Hugging Face, where it has attracted a sizable community of users. Its popularity reflects growing interest in lightweight multimodal models. The GGUF format enables efficient inference on consumer hardware.

items.title: Model: Venastine-Research/Xing4.0-29B-A4B-GGUF
items.summary: Venastine-Research released the Xing4.0-29B-A4B model in GGUF format for text generation, recording 14,361 downloads.
items.detail: The 29‑billion‑parameter model is positioned for high‑quality text generation while remaining compatible with the GGUF runtime. Its download count indicates early adoption among developers experimenting with large language models on edge devices.

items.title: AVR Laptop Pushes the Limits of 8-Bit
items.summary: An AVR‑based laptop demonstrates that an 8‑bit microcontroller can run video, audio, and multitask like a modern notebook.
items.detail: The project showcases the limits of 8‑bit architecture by handling sound playback, video decoding, and interactive applications within a laptop‑sized chassis, highlighting creative engineering on constrained hardware.

items.title: Hackaday Links: October 3, 2026
items.summary: Hackaday's October 3 2026 links roundup mentions a rumor that NASA is attempting to revive the SR‑71 aircraft.
items.detail: The collection links to articles covering aerospace developments, including the SR‑71 revival speculation, alongside other tech news, offering readers a curated snapshot of current interests.

items.title: It’s GW-BASIC, Jim, But Not as We Know It
items.summary: IBM-compatible PCs historically included GW-BASIC in ROM, and continued shipping it after it left ROM.
items.detail: GW-BASIC was the de facto BASIC interpreter for early IBM PCs, providing a simple programming environment that persisted through the transition from ROM to disk-based distribution.

items.title: Motion Control via Belt
items.summary: Tolko created BlobJump, a Raspberry Pi‑based game that uses a belt to encourage physical activity.
items.detail: The project combines motion control hardware with a simple platformer, aiming to make exercise feel like gameplay for children who prefer video games.

items.title: caddyserver/caddy
items.summary: caddyserver/caddy is a fast, extensible multi‑protocol web server with automatic HTTPS.
items.detail: Supporting HTTP/1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3, Caddy simplifies TLS management and offers a modular architecture for plugins, targeting both developers and production deployments.

items.title: ecruells/resident-evil-pc-decomp
items.summary: A decompiled source code of the Resident Evil 1 PC port has been released on GitHub.
items.detail: The repository contains the reverse‑engineered code, enabling analysis of the original game's implementation and facilitating community mods or educational study. It is written in C++ and reflects the game's 1996 architecture.

items.title: getsentry/sentry
items.summary: Sentry provides developer‑first error tracking and performance monitoring as an open‑source platform.
items.detail: The tool aggregates exceptions, performance metrics, and user context, supporting multiple languages and frameworks. It can be self‑hosted or used via SaaS, offering integrations with popular development workflows.
